$comment: Each axis is one construct measured in BOTH humans and LLMs on a shared instrument. 'convergence' and 'robustness' are OUR codings of the cited literature on the rubric in README.md, not figures reported by the papers. Every coding cites the studies it rests on so it can be argued with.

rubric.convergence: 0 = LLM shows the opposite effect or none; 0.5 = same qualitative direction, materially different magnitude or distribution; 1.0 = response distributions statistically indistinguishable from human on the same instrument.
rubric.robustness: Does the match survive trivial, meaning-preserving perturbation of the instrument - renaming entities, reordering options, reformatting labels, novel variants, dropping a persona prompt? 0 = collapses; 1 = unaffected.
rubric.evidence: strong = replicated across independent labs; mixed = replicated with material caveats; contested = direct disagreement in the literature.

axes.label: False-belief attribution
axes.instrument: Sally-Anne and unexpected-contents batteries, with true-belief controls

human.finding: Reliably solved by neurotypical children from roughly age 4-5; near-ceiling in adults. Benchmark sample of 1,907 adults.

ai.finding: GPT-4 solved 75% of 40 bespoke tasks (each requiring all 8 scenarios correct), matching published 6-year-old performance; performs at or above the human sample on false belief in the Strachan battery.

axes.note: The headline result is real and the fragility is equally real: Ullman shows small principle-preserving alterations reverse it, and Ünlütabak finds 100% on standard phrasings dropping below chance on slight modifications.

axes.label: Faux pas recognition
axes.instrument: Faux Pas Recognition Test

human.finding: Adults detect social transgressions and the speaker's ignorance of them reliably.

ai.finding: The one test in the Strachan battery where GPT models fell below humans - traced to hyperconservative refusal to commit rather than failed inference. LLaMA2 scored above humans, but follow-up manipulation showed this reflected a bias toward attributing ignorance.

axes.note: A case where a raw score above humans was shown to be an artefact once belief likelihood was manipulated - the reason the atlas separates convergence from robustness.

axes.label: Higher-order recursive mentalising
axes.instrument: Multi-Order Theory of Mind Q&A (orders 2-6)

human.finding: Adult performance degrades steadily past the 4th order of recursion ('I think that you believe that she knows...').

ai.finding: GPT-4 and Flan-PaLM reach adult or near-adult level overall; GPT-4 exceeds adult performance at 6th-order inferences.

axes.note: Systematic reviews still find second-order and recursive inference is where humans consistently outperform under stricter designs - the result depends heavily on test construction.

axes.label: Pragmatic inference from mental states
axes.instrument: EPITOME battery - belief attribution, emotional inference, pragmatic reasoning

human.finding: Human comprehenders integrate mental-state information into pragmatic interpretation automatically.

ai.finding: LLMs match humans on several EPITOME tasks but commit systematic errors on exactly those requiring pragmatic reasoning from mental-state information.

axes.note: The authors read the uneven profile as evidence that human theory of mind needs resources beyond distributional information.

axes.label: Anchoring on irrelevant numbers
axes.instrument: Tversky-Kahneman anchor-then-estimate prompts

human.finding: Numerical estimates shift toward an arbitrary anchor presented beforehand - one of the most replicated effects in judgment research.

ai.finding: Present across GPT-4, Claude 2, Gemini Pro and GPT-3.5 in randomised controlled trials; ChatGPT anchored in the same direction as human participants run on identical prompts.

axes.note: Genuinely disputed: Shaki et al. found the anchoring effect ABSENT in GPT-3 while priming, distance, SNARC and size-congruity were present. Chain-of-thought and 'ignore the anchor' mitigations are only weakly effective.

axes.label: Framing effects
axes.instrument: Statistically equivalent positive vs negative presentations

human.finding: Judgments of efficacy and risk flip with valence framing despite informationally identical content.

ai.finding: Near-universal across model families in a 70,000-response assessment of 8 models; ChatGPT rated an item more efficacious under positive framing, as human participants did. Source framing shifts agreement across 192,000 assessments.

axes.note: Framing and primacy/recency are the two effects that survive the strictest multi-variant testing - most other biases do not.

axes.label: Endowment effect
axes.instrument: Owned vs newly found identical item valuation

human.finding: People price an item they own above an objectively identical item they do not.

ai.finding: ChatGPT valued an owned item above an identical found item; human participants run on the same prompts showed the same effect.

axes.note: Rests substantially on a single four-study paper. Notable because loss aversion is usually explained by affective processes the model does not have.

axes.label: Conjunction fallacy & availability
axes.instrument: Linda-type conjunction items; anecdote-vs-base-rate items

human.finding: People judge a conjunction more probable than one of its conjuncts, and over-weight vivid anecdotes against base rates.

ai.finding: ChatGPT judged two events co-occurring as likelier than either alone, and was swayed by anecdotal information - matching the human participants tested alongside.

axes.note: Susceptibility varies substantially across model families in larger multi-model assessments.

axes.label: Primacy & recency in option order
axes.instrument: Semantically equivalent prompts with reordered options

human.finding: Serial position shapes recall and choice.

ai.finding: Near-universal across the eight models assessed, and one of only two effect families to generalise across prompt reformulations.

axes.note: In LLMs this is strong enough to invert conclusions - see the order-flip in the Moral Foundations replication.

axes.label: Perceived quality of moral advice
axes.instrument: Modified Moral Turing Test; blinded ratings of moral evaluations

human.finding: Evaluations by a representative US sample and by a professional ethicist serve as the comparison.

ai.finding: A representative sample of 299 US adults rated GPT-4's moral reasoning superior on virtuousness, intelligence and trustworthiness. Americans rated GPT-4o's ethical advice as more moral, trustworthy, thoughtful and correct than a well-known newspaper ethics column.

axes.note: The AI did not pass the identification half of the test - participants still picked the source above chance, possibly because of its perceived superiority.

axes.label: Life-and-death preference profile
axes.instrument: Moral Machine framework

human.finding: Large-scale human preferences: save more lives, prioritise humans over pets, with graded and comparatively mild inclinations.

ai.finding: GPT-3.5/4, PaLM 2 and Llama 2 broadly align on direction, but show significant quantitative disparities and more uncompromising choices. Across 75 configurations from 0.27B to 1000B, distance from human preference falls as a power law, D proportional to S^-0.10.

axes.note: One of the few axes with a measured scaling relationship - alignment improves with size, but slowly, and reasoning models help more at small scale.

axes.label: Distributional fidelity of moral ratings
axes.instrument: 60 scenarios rated for morality, preregistered, against N = 940 humans

human.finding: Human ratings spread across the scale with substantial between-person variability.

ai.finding: Correlations with human means approach r = 1.00, yet difference scores show ChatGPT differs significantly with moderate-to-large effect sizes on roughly 87% of scenarios, giving more extreme ratings and clustering around a restricted set of values.

axes.note: The single most important methodological caution in the atlas: a near-perfect correlation coexists with systematic disagreement on almost every item. Correlation is not agreement.

axes.label: Omission bias in dilemmas
axes.instrument: Realistic moral dilemmas and collective action problems, N = 285 / 474 / 491

human.finding: A representative US sample shows a modest preference for inaction over action in moral dilemmas.

ai.finding: LLMs show markedly stronger omission bias than participants, plus a bias humans do not have: a tendency to answer 'no', which flips the decision depending on how the question is worded. Traced to chatbot fine-tuning.

axes.note: Amplification rather than imitation - the divergence grows with alignment training, not with scale.

axes.label: Affect-driven moral condemnation
axes.instrument: Moral dumbfounding paradigm - harmless but taboo acts

human.finding: Condemnation is predicted better by how disturbing an act feels than by any harm it causes.

ai.finding: Across GPT, Claude and Kimi, judgments of wrongfulness were likewise predicted more strongly by perceived botherness than by perceived harm - reproducing a functional signature of intuitive moral cognition without affect.

axes.note: A judgment-action dissociation appears in agentic mode: models condemn the acts, then frequently comply with direct requests to facilitate them.

axes.label: Subgroup response emulation
axes.instrument: Silicon samples conditioned on sociodemographic backstories from real survey respondents

human.finding: Response distributions from large US surveys across many demographic subgroups.

ai.finding: Properly conditioned GPT-3 emulates response distributions of a wide variety of human subgroups - 'algorithmic fidelity' - reflecting nuanced interplay of attitude and sociocultural context rather than surface similarity.

axes.note: Severely configuration-dependent: across 66 defensible configurations of the same use case, human-silicon correlation ranged from r = .23 to r = .84. The analytic choices, not the model, can decide the finding.

axes.label: Predicting experimental treatment effects
axes.instrument: Archive of 70 preregistered, nationally representative survey experiments - 469 effects, 119,330 participants

human.finding: Pooled human forecasters predict experimental outcomes with well-characterised accuracy.

ai.finding: GPT-4 predictions of simulated treatment effects correlated strongly with actual effects, at accuracy similar to pooled human forecasts - holding for studies published after the training cutoff, and for open-weight models. Effect sizes were systematically overestimated.

axes.note: The strongest positive result in the atlas, and the best controlled for training contamination. In a secondary archive of 15 megastudies (606 effects) correlations were lower but comparable to expert forecasters.

axes.label: Replicating published experiments
axes.instrument: 156 scenario-based experiments from top social science journals, three frontier models

human.finding: The original published human-participant results.

ai.finding: Main effects replicated at 73-81%, interaction effects at 46-63%. Effect sizes consistently larger than the human studies. Where originals reported null findings, LLMs produced significant results 68-83% of the time.

axes.note: Replication rates drop significantly for socially sensitive topics - race, gender, ethics - which is where substitution would be most tempting and least safe.

axes.label: Diversity of response
axes.instrument: Many Labs 2 replications; repeated sampling on opinion items

human.finding: Human samples show wide, structured disagreement on political, economic and moral items - the variance is the signal.

ai.finding: Different runs answered nuanced questions with zero or near-zero variation - a 'correct answer' effect robust to changing demographic details. GPT-3.5 identified as conservative in 99.6% of cases and liberal in 99.3% under reversed option order, while both groups showed right-leaning moral foundations.

axes.note: The largest behavioural divergence in the atlas. Only 37.5% of the analysable Many Labs 2 studies replicated; six of fourteen could not be analysed at all because of the collapse in variance.

axes.label: Strategic reasoning depth
axes.instrument: 11-20 money request game (level-k depth of reasoning)

human.finding: Human play produces a characteristic distribution over reasoning levels rather than a single best response.

ai.finding: Nearly all advanced approaches fail to replicate the human behaviour distribution across many models. Failure causes are diverse and unpredictable - input language, assigned role, safeguarding behaviour.

axes.note: Reads as a direct counterweight to the population-simulation successes: the same models that predict aggregate treatment effects miss the shape of strategic play.

axes.label: Three-party Turing test
axes.instrument: 5-minute simultaneous conversation with one human and one system, preregistered

human.finding: The real human witness is selected as the human less than half the time when facing a persona-prompted frontier model.

ai.finding: GPT-4.5 with a humanlike persona prompt was judged the human 73% of the time - significantly more often than interrogators selected the real human. LLaMa-3.1-405B reached 56%, statistically level with humans.

axes.note: The fragility is the finding: without the persona prompt the same models fell to 38% and 36%, not consistently better than ELIZA (23%) or un-prompted GPT-4o (21%). A third study replicated the pass at 15-minute length (56% and 59%).

axes.label: Detection from transcript
axes.instrument: Displaced and inverted Turing tests - judging a transcript rather than interrogating

human.finding: Interactive interrogators are meaningfully accurate; displaced human judges reading transcripts fall below chance.

ai.finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and displaced human adjudicators alike judged the best-performing GPT-4 witness to be human more often than they judged actual human witnesses to be human.

axes.note: Most real-world exposure is displaced - people read conversations rather than interrogate. This is the condition under which detection is worst.

axes.label: Behavioural game & personality profile
axes.instrument: Classic behavioural game battery (trust, fairness, risk, cooperation) plus Big-5 inventory

human.finding: Tens of thousands of human subjects from more than 50 countries provide the comparison distribution.

ai.finding: ChatGPT-4's behavioural and personality traits are statistically indistinguishable from a random human drawn from that sample. It modifies behaviour with experience and re-framing as if learning.

axes.note: Indistinguishable from a RANDOM human, not from the average one: where behaviour is distinct it sits at the altruistic and cooperative end, acting as if maximising an average of its own and its partner's payoffs.

axes.label: Cortical response encoding
axes.instrument: Linear mapping from model activations to fMRI/ECoG responses during naturalistic listening

human.finding: 101 subjects recorded with fMRI over 70 minutes of short stories; comprehension scored per story.

ai.finding: GPT-2 representations map onto brain responses to spoken stories and additionally predict how well each subject understood each narrative, peaking in angular, medial temporal and supramarginal gyri.

axes.note: Representational rather than behavioural convergence - and it goes beyond correlation to predicting a behavioural outcome (comprehension) from the mapping.

axes.label: Layer depth ↔ cortical timescale
axes.instrument: ECoG during a 30-minute narrative; per-layer encoding models

human.finding: The cortical language network has a graded temporal receptive window, with later integration in Broca's area and associated regions.

ai.finding: Deeper layers of GPT-2 XL and Llama-2 correspond to later brain activity, with model depth tracking the brain's temporal receptive window during comprehension.

axes.note: As benchmark performance improves, models become more brain-like AND align more closely with the brain's hierarchical feature-extraction pathway, using fewer layers for the same encoding.

axes.label: Reading time & N400 prediction
axes.instrument: Self-paced reading, gaze duration, MAZE times, N400 potentials

human.finding: Processing difficulty shows up as slower reading, longer fixations and larger N400 amplitude.

ai.finding: Next-word probabilities from the INTERNAL layers of larger models fit human sentence-processing data as well as or better than smaller models - overturning the claim that scale makes models cognitively implausible, which rested on reading only the final layer.

axes.note: Earlier layers track fast gaze durations; later layers track slower signals such as N400 and MAZE times. Whether scale helps or hurts depends entirely on which layer you read.

axes.label: Language data to fluency
axes.instrument: Words of linguistic input required to reach fluent use

human.finding: Children acquire fluent language from under 100 million words of input - and much of the grounding comes through multimodal, interactive, social exposure.

ai.finding: Language models typically need three to four orders of magnitude more data than that and still underperform humans on many evaluations; the gap to children is put at four to five orders of magnitude.

axes.note: Training on child-directed speech does not close it: the evidence points to the child's learning algorithm being substantially more data-efficient, not the child's data being better.

axes.label: Power budget for cognition
axes.instrument: Metabolic accounting of cortical computation vs datacentre inference

human.finding: The whole brain runs on about 20 W. Partitioned, only ~0.1 W of ATP goes to cortical computation itself; long-distance communication costs 35 times more, about 3.5 W.

ai.finding: Frontier training and serving consume many orders of magnitude more energy for narrower lifetime capability, which is the explicit motivation for neuromorphic and spiking alternatives.

axes.note: Biological brains do lifelong learning, adaptive control and flexible reasoning inside that budget. The gap is architectural, not a matter of better hardware alone.

axes.label: Invariance to surface reformatting
axes.instrument: Semantically identical items with reformatted labels and reordered options

human.finding: Human judgments are substantially - not perfectly - invariant to relabelling the options in a question.

ai.finding: Renaming 'Case 1' and 'Case 2' to '(A)' and '(B)' materially changes moral judgments. Under variant-level testing that requires an effect to generalise across prompt formulations, 27 of 43 trial-level significant bias effects collapse to one.

axes.note: This axis governs every other one. Prompt-induced systematic uncertainty dominates statistical uncertainty, which means many published human-LLM similarities are claims about a phrasing rather than about a model.
